notes.meaning: Elizur gave a silver platter and a silver bowl, both filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering. He also presented a gold dish filled with sweet incense. These valuable dishes and grain gifts were set apart for regular worship in the Tabernacle.

Elizur brought animals for three different kinds of sacrifices: burnt offerings to show total dedication, a goat for a sin offering to seek cleansing, and several animals for a peace offering. The peace offering provided a sacred meal shared between God, the priests, and the people. Even during this happy celebration, the sin offering reminded Israel of their constant need for God's forgiveness.

On the fifth day, Shelumiel stepped forward to bring the dedication gift for the tribe of Simeon. Simeon was camped on the south side of the Tabernacle next to Reuben. Each leader came forward in an orderly march, following the camp arrangement God had given.

Shelumiel presented a silver platter and a silver bowl filled with flour and oil, along with a gold dish full of incense. His gift was identical in size and value to the gifts from the other tribes. This showed that every tribe had the same standing and duty before the Lord.

Shelumiel brought a bull, a ram, and a lamb for a burnt offering, a goat for a sin offering, and many animals for peace offerings. These sacrifices covered every part of worship, from seeking pardon for sin to enjoying fellowship with the Lord. They expressed Simeon's full devotion to God's dwelling place.

On the sixth day, Eliasaph brought the gift for the tribe of Gad. His father Deuel is also called Reuel elsewhere in Scripture. Gad completed the southern group of tribes that camped together around the holy tent.

Eliasaph presented a silver platter and bowl filled with fine flour and oil, as well as a gold dish containing incense. Every metal dish was weighed according to the official standard of the sanctuary. These gifts provided both the sacred dishes and the ingredients needed for daily offerings.

Eliasaph offered the required animals for a burnt offering, a sin offering, and peace offerings. Scripture repeats the details for each tribe to show that God values the personal devotion and obedience of every group. The meat of the peace offerings was eaten in a joyful feast celebrating peace with God.

On the seventh day, Elishama brought the dedication gift for Ephraim, the head tribe on the west side of the camp. This was the seventh day of the dedication ceremony, which may or may not have fallen on the weekly Sabbath. Either way, bringing gifts to dedicate the altar and worshiping the Lord was fitting work for any holy day.

Elishama presented the silver platter and bowl filled with fine flour and oil, along with the gold dish of incense. Ephraim gave the exact same items and weights as the tribes before them. Even though Ephraim was a prominent and favored tribe, they gave the same tribute, showing that all tribes were equal in God's eyes.

Elishama completed his gift with animals for a burnt offering, a sin offering, and peace offerings. These sacrifices reminded the people that close fellowship with God begins with atonement, which means being reconciled through sacrifice. This concluded the seventh day of dedication.

On the eighth day, Gamaliel brought the offering for the tribe of Manasseh. Manasseh camped beside Ephraim on the west side of the Tabernacle, as both tribes were descended from Joseph. Gamaliel took his place in the orderly sequence God commanded.

Gamaliel gave a silver platter and bowl containing fine flour mixed with oil, plus a gold dish filled with incense. These offerings supplied the priests with items needed for the Tabernacle's ongoing grain and incense services. The exact weights recorded in the text reflect careful records kept for the sanctuary.

Gamaliel presented the animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings, finishing the gifts for Manasseh. The peace offerings supplied plenty of food for the leaders and people to celebrate together in God's presence. Manasseh showed the same generous heart and reverent obedience as the rest of Israel.
